questions.q: Is Briarcliff Outdoor Gear, the company in this case study, a real business?
options: No — it's explicitly described as a fictional, illustrative composite scenario
Yes — it is a real, named outdoor retailer
Yes — it is a real company whose name was changed for privacy
The lesson does not say whether it is real or fictional
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly labels Briarcliff Outdoor Gear as fictional and illustrative, consistent with this catalog's policy against presenting invented scenarios as real.

questions.q: What was the root problem at Briarcliff, per this lesson?
options: The AWS footprint inherited from an acquisition was a black box to the security team, so nobody could confidently answer who could access customer browsing data across both clouds
The company had no cloud infrastructure of any kind
All of Briarcliff's data was accidentally deleted
Briarcliff used only AWS and had no Azure presence at all
questions.explain: Azure access reviews were routine, but the AWS side — inherited from an acquisition — had no one on the security team with credentials and only outdated documentation.

questions.q: How did Briarcliff fix the identity gap between Azure and AWS, per this lesson?
options: By federating Entra ID into AWS IAM roles, making Entra ID the one source of truth for identity on both clouds
By creating a brand-new, separate AWS IAM user for every Azure employee individually
By ignoring AWS identity entirely since it was a smaller system
By migrating the entire AWS analytics platform onto Azure immediately
questions.explain: Federating Entra ID into AWS IAM roles meant access reviews could run through one identity system and one quarterly process instead of two unconnected ones.

questions.q: How did Briarcliff address the policy-drift risk from Lesson 21 in this case study?
options: They translated the Azure Policy encryption/access requirement into an equivalent AWS Organizations service control policy as part of the same change, not a follow-up ticket
They deleted the Azure Policy entirely to avoid any mismatch
They assumed AWS would automatically copy whatever Azure Policy enforced
They did not address policy drift in this case study
questions.explain: Treating the AWS-side translation as a required step of the same change — not something that could slip into a later backlog — is exactly the fix Lesson 21 pointed toward.

questions.q: According to this lesson's closing point, what did Briarcliff's fix actually require?
options: Applying what Chapters 1 through 4 already taught, once per cloud, with a deliberately and actively maintained map connecting the two
Migrating every AWS workload onto Azure immediately
Purchasing a brand-new, all-in-one universal multi-cloud governance product
Shutting down the AWS analytics pipeline entirely
questions.explain: The lesson's point is that multi-cloud governance doesn't need a new tool or a migration — it needs the same governance discipline applied to both clouds, with an actively maintained control map connecting them.
